canberra.title: ‘Significant and competing expectations’: Parking rules at Goulburn’s hospital, CBD changed
canberra.snippet: Hospital parking permits are officially dead in Goulburn as a NSW Southern Tablelands council overhauls street parking restrictions. In e...
canberra.content:
Next time you want to park in Goulburn, check whether the restrictions have changed. Photo: James Coleman.

Hospital parking permits are officially dead in Goulburn as a NSW Southern Tablelands council overhauls street parking restrictions.

In early 2026, Goulburn Mulwaree Council (GMC) began public consultation around parking restrictions in the town’s CBD and the hospital precinct.

In their comments about the feedback, in meeting papers, staff wrote that there were “significant and competing expectations” around what the public wanted.

“Nevertheless, the review confirms that the fundamental principles underpinning the exhibited proposal remain valid … and parking turnover remains critical to both hospital access and economic activity.”

Parking restrictions around the hospital are set to start from 8 am (as opposed to 6 am previously), Monday to Friday.

“[This decision] more closely aligns with contemporary hospital activity and parking demand whilst providing greater flexibility for surrounding residents, visitors, carers and tradespersons,” the papers state.

“This allows most routine residential activities, including family visits, home maintenance and trade-related work, to occur without unnecessary parking restrictions outside weekday business hours.”

Under the newly adopted restrictions, the council formally scrapped a permit system around the Goulburn Base Hospital Precinct.

The permits haven’t been enforced since late 2024, with some being copied and shared.

A staff member acknowledged that the move would need to come with an information campaign to make sure the community was aware of the change.

“Unfortunately, for the last couple of years, because we haven’t been able to enforce anything happening in the hospital precinct, that has led people to have certain behaviours,” he told the meeting.

“We haven’t been able to call them out, whereas now we will be. We’re going to have a lot of communications and messaging that we expect them to circulate to staff and visitors.”

The changes will see sections of nearby Prell and Show streets changed to two-hour parking slots.

The hospital site on Albert Street will also be two-hour parking.

Parking restrictions were left largely unchanged within the town’s CBD, though the timed parking along Verner Street, which was to be scrapped, was kept.

Unlike the hospital precinct, the council kept the operating hours for the restrictions the same.

It means the restrictions are in place between 8:30 am and 6:30 pm from Mondays to Fridays, and until 12:30 pm on Saturdays.

According to the council documents, there are about 3110 parking spaces within the CBD (including private and council-operated sources).

The motion also flags further changes on the horizon.

It means GMC will investigate the need for the southbound bus zone at Auburn and Verner streets, including whether part of the area should be converted to angle parking.

The council is also set to start talks with NSW Health and other government agencies about how to ensure hospital staff have safe parking.

It will also investigate options for improved short-term parking arrangements adjacent to Goulburn High School.

The council agreed to reinstate bus zones outside Bourke Street Public School.

A full list of the key changes is available on the council’s website.

Original Article published by Claire Sams on About Regional.

canberra.title: Cloud over The Markets Residences in Belconnen as company goes bust
canberra.snippet: The company behind Belconnen’s under-construction Markets Residences has entered receivership after months of pushback from off-the-plan ...
canberra.content:
The Markets Residences in Belconnen. There has been speculation about its future for months. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

The company behind Belconnen’s under-construction Markets Residences has entered receivership after months of pushback from off-the-plan buyers who claim they were misled over bedroom counts, leaving some struggling to secure finance.

Receivers Costas Niccodemou and James Sekhas from Newpoint Advisory took charge of Beldev Nominees on Wednesday (25 November), according to ASIC documents.

Beldev’s directors are prominent Canberra developers Peter Micalos and Mena Ibrahim, whose IP Property is behind several other projects in Canberra. Mr Micalos is managing director and Mr Ibrahim executive director, respectively, of IP Property.

The builder is reputable firm Icon Construction.

Rumours have been swirling around the future of the 10-storey, 326-apartment project on the corner of Belconnen Way and Lathlain Street, which has been dogged by delays and, at one time, even intimidation by bikies.

There have been ongoing concerns about buyers seeking to get out of their contracts, threatening the viability of the project, which was expected to be completed in the first quarter of next year.

Many had commenced action through Adero Law, upset about purchasing what they believed was a three or four-bedroom apartment but was now shown on plans as two and three beds with a study or habitable room.

There were also concern that this would affect valuations and the ability obtain finance.

After a meeting was held in August, the developer moved to reassure buyers that units would be delivered as per contracts and all applicable legislation.

Buyer Janine Haskins, who Region has previously spoken to about delays and changes to the project design, has been pursuing rescission herself and now fears for her deposit.

She said the whole ordeal had been an absolute nightmare – stress, distress and everything in between.

“From paying a sizeable deposit, i.e. our life savings of $50,000 on what we thought would be our forever home, we now have to rethink our retirement plans and remain unsure if we will receive our deposit back,” she said.

“Disappointing is an understatement.”

In recent weeks, concerns also had been raised about a shortfall in visitor parking.

Affected buyers should seek legal advice, review the contract and confirm their deposit is protected.

With the project at such a late stage, the receivers will be endeavouring to have it completed and compliant.

Icon broke ground on the project in April 2023. In 2024, a dispute among the project joint venture partners resulted in developer Shane Anderson being ousted, resulting in protracted legal action.

In August, Mr Anderson was convicted of criminal contempt over a campaign of intimidation against his former business partners that included an outlaw motorcycle gang ordering the building site be shut down.

Mr Anderson has appealed against the NSW Supreme Court decision.

canberra.title: Last-minute legal bid delays sentencing for Griffith winemaker accused of $12 million GST fraud
canberra.snippet: A last-minute legal application in the NSW District Court has delayed the sentencing of former Griffith winemaker Aaron Salvestrin until ...
canberra.content:
Aaron Salvestrin was once touted as a rising star of the wine industry. Photo: Sans Pareil.

A last-minute legal application in the NSW District Court has delayed the sentencing of former Griffith winemaker Aaron Salvestrin until 2027, months after he admitted his business altered supplier invoices to fraudulently claim millions of dollars in GST refunds.

The 32-year-old was scheduled to be sentenced at Sydney’s Downing Centre on Thursday (26 November) before Judge Kenneth Averre, having pleaded guilty in June to two counts of dishonestly obtaining a gain from a Commonwealth entity and one count of using a forged document to induce a public official to accept it as genuine.

The three certified Commonwealth offences relate to the collapse of his Hanwood-based winery, Sans Pareil Estate, which was paid more than $12 million in Australian Taxation Office GST refunds, despite reporting annual turnover of less than $2 million.

However, sentencing submissions were halted at the outset when Salvestrin’s defence barrister, Russ Johnstone, handed up a late notice of motion seeking orders over materials already on the court file, as well as further documents arriving in a sealed envelope during the morning.

“The notice of motion itself should be self-explanatory, but the basis for it may need some explanation,” Mr Johnstone told the court.

Commonwealth prosecutor Patrick Dixon indicated the Crown opposed the motion.

Before Mr Johnstone outlined the basis for the application or Judge Averre ruled on it, Region’s audio-visual link to the courtroom was abruptly terminated.

Official court records subsequently confirmed that sentencing did not conclude on Thursday, with Judge Averre marking the matter part-heard and adjourning it to Albury District Court on 8 March 2027.

This means Salvestrin will remain on bail under the same conditions he was placed on at the first hearing in August 2025.

The Griffith man is to report to Dee Why Police Station (in Sydney) once daily between 8 am and 8 pm.

He was also ordered to surrender any passports he held to any police officer at the Dee Why Police Area Command within 12 hours; not to apply for any passport or travel document; and not to enter any point of departure (such as an airport) in Australia.

Under his bail conditions, he must remain within the Sydney Northern Beaches postcode 2099, but can travel to Griffith provided he notifies police of his intention 24 hours in advance.

Region first exposed the winery’s collapse in an exclusive investigation in 2023 and has followed the saga through three years of reporting, including separate civil and criminal proceedings.

According to a statement of facts tendered in court, Salvestrin registered Sans Pareil as an export business and told the ATO it was selling large quantities of wine to a European buyer.

The winery did not produce its own wine; instead, it bought bulk wine from other producers and sold it under its own brand.

Because GST generally does not apply to goods exported overseas, Sans Pareil could claim refunds for GST it had supposedly paid when buying bulk wine from Australian suppliers.

Salvestrin admitted using PDF software to alter genuine supplier invoices, inflating the amounts shown so the company could claim GST refunds it was not entitled to.

In one instance, the ATO paid Sans Pareil $1.73 million after the winery submitted an invoice claiming it purchased $19 million worth of wine.

The South Australian supplier later told the ATO it had never issued an invoice for that amount and that the document submitted contained an incorrect Australian Business Number (ABN).

Court documents revealed the ATO made 15 GST refund payments to Sans Pareil between April 2021 and June 2022, totalling more than $12 million.

The ATO eventually audited the company, which collapsed into liquidation in October 2022 with an alleged $32 million debt to the tax office, including interest and penalties.

Among the assets sold during the liquidation was a 2014 McLaren P1 supercar signed by Formula One star Daniel Ricciardo. It fetched $1.47 million, well below what Salvestrin was understood to have paid for it.

In March 2024, the NSW Supreme Court ordered Salvestrin to repay more than $8.4 million to creditors after finding he had made unreasonable director-related transactions while running the business.

He declared himself bankrupt seven days later.

The criminal case was a separate matter that commenced in August 2025, with the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions initially bringing 17 charges before withdrawing most of them after Salvestrin entered his guilty pleas. The case has been delayed multiple times since it began.

When Salvestrin launched Sans Pareil Estate in 2018, the 24-year-old Hanwood local was considered a rising star of the Riverina wine industry.

Armed with a TAFE certificate in wine operations, he appeared to build a multi-million-dollar export business within four years, with the brand claiming to export to 10 countries.

He was even praised by the NSW Government agency Destination NSW for his “rule-breaking wine” and “untraditional methods”.

Original Article published by Oliver Jacques on Region Riverina.

canberra.title: The biggest school budget losers revealed as Minister relents
canberra.snippet: Majura Primary School will take the hardest hit among 18 schools facing budget cuts of more than 5 per cent in 2027, with funding project...
canberra.content:
26 November 2026

Start the conversation

Education Minister will be talking to parents at Majura Primary School, which is taking the biggest funding cut in 2027. Photo: ACT Government.

Majura Primary School will take the hardest hit among 18 schools facing budget cuts of more than 5 per cent in 2027, with funding projected to fall by $1,230,524, or 13.4 per cent.

The ACT Government has released public school budget data for the past four years, as well as the 2027 projections, in the wake of a media and community outcry over its limited release of information and refusal to name schools last week, despite a commitment to be transparent about the funding arrangements.

The data, based on comparing schools’ 2026 expenditure with their 2027 projected budgets, shows that 42 schools will receive less funding and 50 schools will receive more, with 22 increases of more than 5 per cent.

Majura and Latham Primary School (-12.96%) face the sharpest reductions, followed by Theodore Primary (-11.38%), Gowrie Primary (-10.41%), and Macquarie Primary (-10.29%).

In dollar terms, Majura, The Canberra College (-$1,152,48, -7.54%), and Evelyn Scott School (-$1,102,696, -8.77%) are the top three, followed closely by Palmerston District Primary School with a cut of $976,087 (-9.97%).

The data shows that primary schools bear the brunt of the redistribution of funding, designed to create a more equitable school system, with 16 facing cuts greater than 5 per cent.

Malkara School will receive the biggest funding boost, rising almost by a fifth (+19.09%, +$1,304,625).

All the specialist schools have been given hefty increases.

Funding will rise for The Woden School by 13.84 per cent (+$995,249), Cranleigh School by 13.09 per cent (+$895,171) and Black Mountain School by 11.34 per cent (+$1,165,328).

Melba Copland Secondary School has the biggest dollar increase, at nearly $2 million (+$1,832,308, +11.62%), while Wanniassa School also topped the million mark with a $1,164,293 increase (+11.32%).

Other winners by percentage are Gilmore Primary (+14.92%, +$422,857), Arawang Primary (+14.01%, +$737,878), Richardson Primary (+13.15%, +$441,293), Calwell High (+13.01%, +$899,930), and Lyons Early Childhood (+11.80%, +$283,795).

From a district perspective, the biggest funding cuts are in North Canberra and Gungahlin, where there are falling enrolments as the demographic wave passes.

Education Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith said the government recognised the community, media and Legislative Assembly wanted more information – and acknowledged it would have to be released anyway.

But she remained unrepentant about holding back the names of schools and full numbers last week when principals received their projected budgets. At the time, she said she wanted to protect principals, citing psychosocial concerns, and to avoid a league table of schools being published.

It provoked a media backlash and groups such as Parents ACT said the community deserved to know.

“I’d rather that I have bad headlines than principals have all of those challenging conversations,” Ms Stephen-Smith told Region.

She said principals had now had a week to assess their budgets and talk to school boards, their P&Cs, and any parents, aware that the government would be releasing this information.

Ms Stephen-Smith stressed that schools had been given projected budgets, which could change on updated enrolment information from the February census. Final budgets would be completed in March or April 2027, and these would also be published along with the final expenditure for 2026.

Acting Deputy Director-General Angela Spence indicated that most projections would be on target, with about 12 schools being monitored for enrolment fluctuations.

“There are some schools in some locations that have demographic drops,” she said.

“In the Gungahlin area we’re seeing a shift come as the kids are getting older and they’re going off to colleges, or going between primary and high school.

“But from an enrolment projection perspective, most of our schools are very stable.”

Ms Spence said savings would come from better management of class sizes and staff, as well as some schools having to trim their extracurricular offerings.

She said this meant maximising class sizes within the limits agreed with the teachers’ union to free up staff, getting school leaders to spend more time in the classroom and using more combined classes.

“Some young people may have been in a class with 10 kids in it. They’ll be in a class that might have 18, 19, 20 students if they’re in K to 3.

Learning support assistant staff would also be moved to where they were needed in the system.

Ms Stephen-Smith reiterated that the new funding arrangements were about fairness across the system.

“This is about ensuring all of our schools are funded on an equitable basis and that funding distribution is fair across our schools,” she said.

“Everyone would be aware that some schools are offering more in extracurricular and enrichment activities than others are able to do.

“We want to ensure that those schools that have been a bit restricted in their capacity to offer those things also have an opportunity to do that, and that is about funding, but it’s also about staffing, and then that does go back to the teacher mobility and ensuring that we’re having our experienced teachers spread across all of our schools fairly.”

Ms Stephen-Smith said she believed parents recognised that the whole system needed to be funded equitably.

Majura Primary, which will take the biggest cut, had invited her to talk to parents, something she was open to with all school communities.

“I see that as a core part of the job,” she said.

“I’m not aware that I’ve been invited by any other P&Cs at this point, but if they do want to have a conversation, I’m happy to do that.”

ACT Parents Executive Officer Veronica Elliot said her organisation had developed a school funding explorer to help families make sense of the published figures.

Ms Elliott said they could find their school, explore funding and enrolment changes from 2023 to 2027, and compare schools of the same type.

She said ACT Parents supported fair funding that directed resources where they were needed.

But schools served different communities with different needs, so equity was about more than every school receiving the same amount.

“The explorer makes the figures easier to understand, but it cannot tell us whether funding is sufficient to meet students’ needs,” Ms Elliott said.

“Families still need clear, school-specific information about what changes will mean in practice.”

Note: Whitlam School has no funding allocations listed for 2026 or 2027 and is excluded from the change calculations.

canberra.title: Motorcyclist killed in Hindmarsh Drive crash, bystanders thanked for trying to help
canberra.snippet: Bystanders have been thanked for trying to save the life of a 40-year-old motorcyclist killed in a crash on Hindmarsh Drive in Phillip th...
canberra.content:
A Waramanga man has died following a motorcycle crash in Phillip. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

Bystanders have been thanked for trying to save the life of a 40-year-old motorcyclist killed in a crash on Hindmarsh Drive in Phillip this afternoon (26 November).

Emergency services were called to the eastbound lanes of Hindmarsh Drive between Melrose Drive and Ball Street at about 12:30 pm.

There, they found a Honda motorcycle that had left the roadway, and the rider had hit a pole.

Bystanders were performing CPR on the unconscious Waramanga man when paramedics arrived.

“Resuscitation efforts continued on the way to the hospital,” ACT Ambulance Services duty commander Lynda Hawkins said.

“[He was taken] to hospital in a critical condition.”

Investigations are underway into the circumstances surrounding the crash. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

The man is the 14th person to die on Canberra’s roads this year.

ACT Policing’s Major Collision Team is now investigating the circumstances surrounding the crash.

Detective Sergeant Jonathan Turkich urged all road users to make sure they were being as safe as they possibly could be.

“I’m getting quite exhausted with coming and analysing these scenes and looking at them – it is our job, but it affects everybody,” he said.

“It affects witnesses, it affects our emergency services partners, it affects the community. They’re just tragic.

“I really want to implore Canberra motorists, as we come up to the holiday period, to look after each other and look after themselves on the road.”

Bystanders tried to revive the rider. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

Det Sgt Turkich confirmed the rider appeared to be wearing appropriate protective gear, though its effectiveness will form part of the investigation. Investigators will also examine whether other vehicles were involved, alongside potential factors such as speeding, impairment, or a medical episode.

“As collision investigators, we don’t like to rule anything out straight away. We go through a methodical process through the investigation,” Det Sgt Turkich said.

“But when you look at what the ‘fatal five’ are, we generally find that in most collisions, one of those fatal five is a factor in the death.

“The saddest part is that most collisions are completely, completely avoidable.”

The fatal five are speeding, alcohol and drug impaired driving, driver distraction, failure to obey traffic lights and signs, and not wearing a seatbelt.

Cmdr Hawkins commended the bystanders who tried to save the rider’s life.

“We say thank you very much for performing [CPR],” she said.

“No doubt they will be suffering a bit this afternoon as well, so hopefully they have some support for themselves.”

Anyone who witnessed the crash or has dashcam footage of the crash or rider immediately before 12.30 pm today (26 November) has been urged to contact ACT Policing on 131 444 or Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000, quoting P2508161.

australia.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon used his service weapon to murder two men. Did NSW police recruiters miss any red flags?
australia.snippet: Video of convicted double murderer shows him in 2020 deploying a Taser at close range to an Indigenous man’s face, chest and neck Get our...
australia.content:
Beau Lamarre-Condon, the double murderer who killed Jesse Baird and Luke Davies while he was a serving New South Wales police officer, had been under review by the force for repeatedly using his Taser on a man four years before the killings.

On Wednesday, he was convicted after a 12-person jury found he had murdered both men with his police service weapon on 19 February 2024.

During his 10-week trial, the prosecution alleged Lamarre-Condon had misused his authority as a police officer to obtain CCTV footage of Baird, who he had casually dated; stolen training bullets from the police; and taken a weapon from a police station to use in his crimes.

The NSW police commissioner, Mal Lanyon, has offered his thoughts to the families of Baird and Davies and condemned Lamarre-Condon.

“The actions for which Mr Lamarre-Condon has now been convicted are abhorrent and completely at odds with his oath of office as a police officer which he undertook. His actions are unacceptable to me, the NSW Police Force and to any member of our community,” he said in a statement.

“I also wish to acknowledge the professionalism and dedication of those officers who conducted the investigation into the deaths of Mr Baird and Mr Davies.”

But the trial’s revelations have raised questions about how NSW police recruits its officers.

“If police recruitment processes and then police professional standards can let this guy get through all the gates, we need to review our checks and balances,” Dr Justin Ellis, a University of Newcastle criminology lecturer, told Guardian Australia.

“Authority figures are expected to meet higher ethical and behavioural standards, and in this case, the additional responsibility that comes with being a police officer.”

The circumstances surrounding Lamarre-Condon’s recruitment and ongoing employment are being examined by a coronial inquest and a critical incident investigation, NSW police said in a statement.

Terry Goldsworthy, a criminologist at Bond University and former detective, suggested the force revisit Lamarre-Condon’s assessment to see whether any red flags were missed.

He added that Lamarre-Condon’s case is an “extraordinary exception” rather than indicative of systemic issues in the police.

But Ellis believes this type of framing, which narrows focus to individual actors, must be taken into wider consideration of the police processes that “may have enabled the ‘bad apple’ to be in place and to stay in place”.

Separate from the police response to the murders, recruitment processes have been probed as part of a broader independent cultural review, released in June.

It recommended the NSW police force change testing and vetting processes that unintentionally exclude capable candidates, following recent downturns in applicants.

Applicants to the police academy are required to undertake a psychometric test, but former police officer turned criminologist at Macquarie University, Vincent Hurley, said “anyone can bluff a questionnaire”.

He said police should, and may already have, reviewed Lamarre-Condon’s psychometric testing, as well as any complaints by the public or other officers about his behaviour.

Years of staff shortages are placing pressure on recruiting and retaining officers, which can lead to complaints being overlooked, Hurley said.

Four years before the murders and about three years into his policing career, Lamarre-Condon became the subject of an internal police review after video emerged of him repeatedly deploying a Taser on an Indigenous man in the face, chest and neck.

During the June 2020 incident, Lamarre-Condon yells, “If you move, I will Taser you,” before pulling the man to the ground and firing his stun gun.

The man says: “Are you serious? I’m trying to protect my face, I’m not even fighting you.”

An internal review by NSW police cleared Lamarre-Condon of any wrongdoing, finding that he had complied with policy and training guidelines, The Australian reported.

‘Haters like to hate’

Police faced intense scrutiny after the murders first occurred in 2024.

Then police commissioner Karen Webb came under fire when she described the killings as a “crime of passion” and responded to criticism by saying: “There will always be haters. Haters like to hate. Isn’t that what Taylor [Swift] says?”

During the trial, it was revealed Baird did not believe he could report Lamarre-Condon’s stalking and controlling behaviour to law enforcement because of his role in the police.

Even if he did report the officer, Hurley said there was a chance police may not have taken him seriously because he did not fit the mould of a “stereotypical” victim of such behaviour – referring to the fact he was not in a heterosexual relationship.

Hurley said Baird and Davies’ deaths were a “wake-up call” for police in how such matters are handled.

The independent NSW MP Alex Greenwich, who helped facilitate a 2024 vigil for Baird and Davies, said after the verdicts: “This tragic and heartbreaking violent crime tells us we need to do everything we can do to increase awareness, reporting, support and access to justice for LGBTQ victims of stalking and violence.”

People in the LGBTQ+ community have long faced discrimination when engaging with police and the justice system, with a 2022 special commission of inquiry into LGBTQ+ hate crimes revealing police reluctance to thoroughly investigate homicides and assaults involving gay men and transgender women.

Ellis, who is part of a NSW police force taskforce established in response to inquiry, said police have an opportunity to renew their engagement strategies with the LGBTQ+ community.

“The more that they’re trusted and people have confidence in them, the more likely [people] are to report to the police.”

In the wake of the murders, NSW police reviewed and implemented changes to the force’s firearms policies and procedures, which have been welcomed by Hurley and Goldsworthy.

At the time of Lamarre-Condon’s arrest, the NSW police force launched its critical incident investigation, which is ongoing and being monitored by the Law Enforcement Conduct Commission.

The investigation will also be reviewed by the police’s professional standards command.

Eventual findings from the ongoing coronial inquest may offer recommendations for the police.

australia.title: Donations to One Nation from two Gina Rinehart associates to be probed by electoral authorities
australia.snippet: Exclusive : Australian Electoral Commission to review $1m in donations to Pauline Hanson-led party from Adam Giles and Ian Plimer Get our...
australia.content:
Major donations from close associates of One Nation’s billionaire benefactor, Gina Rinehart, will be reviewed by the Australian Electoral Commission (AEC) amid concerns they were made on behalf of a third party.

The special minister of state, Don Farrell, said on Thursday that information about two $500,000 donations made to the Pauline Hanson-led party could be subject to further regulatory action if they are found not to comply with provisions in the Electoral Act.

In April, Hanson thanked two of Rinehart’s closest associates and senior executives for their “investment” in the party at the same time as she unveiled a private plane gifted to her by Rinehart.

The geologist Ian Plimer, who is an executive with Hancock Energy and known for his climate denialism, and Adam Giles, the head of Hancock Agriculture and former Northern Territory chief minister, each donated $500,000 to One Nation.

At the time, Hanson thanked “two wonderful patriotic Australians” for the combined $1m in contributions.

The money – and the use of the new Cirrus SR22 G7 plane – which can retail for about $2.1m, prompted Labor to accuse One Nation of being “a wholly owned subsidiary of Gina Rinehart”.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

A question on notice about the donations from Plimer and Giles asked if the government had “any concerns that these donations were made on behalf of a third party”.

In answer, Farrell said the Electoral Act required relevant disclosures to be made within 2025-26 annual financial disclosure returns to the AEC, due earlier this month.

He said information about donations and in-kind support to political parties, including One Nation, would be published on the AEC’s transparency register on 1 February.

“The AEC will examine disclosures and determine whether further regulatory action is required,” Farrell said.

Guardian Australia has reported extensively on Hanson’s links to Rinehart, including her repeated failures to properly declare free flights on the mining magnate’s private jet.

Hancock Prospecting and One Nation were contacted for comment on Thursday.

The Coalition raised concerns with the federal government about whether Plimer and Giles had made the donations on behalf of a third party, asking if the source of the money would be investigated.

Crossbencher David Pocock also sought more information about the donations, using a parliamentary question on notice to ask if the AEC could investigate their source.

Guardian Australia reported in September that James Ashby, formerly Hanson’s chief of staff and now the party’s national director, drives a new Ford Ranger that was “personally” gifted to One Nation by Giles in April.

Hanson said the vehicle would help the party’s campaign efforts and “provides us the presence we need in the lead up to the next federal election”.

Hanson celebrated the defection of Liberal Leah Blyth to One Nation on Thursday, suggesting the senator would “build on One Nation’s expanding support” in South Australia.

The defection sparked recriminations from within the Coalition, even as Blyth struggled to justify her move to a party she has previously criticised – and as she fumbled key policy positions held by Hanson.

The Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, called Blyth “a turncoat” while the deputy Liberal leader, Jane Hume, said her former colleague “wasn’t a big contributor” to the Coalition.

In an interview with the Australian Financial Review on Thursday, Hanson insisted she was not controlled by Rinehart, pointing to her party’s opposition to the Australia-European Union free trade agreement.

Rinehart would benefit from the deal, including provisions to ease tariffs on beef and critical minerals.

australia.title: ‘Disaster’ unfolding as Sydney fire ant outbreak partly blamed on ignored biosecurity recommendations
australia.snippet: Farmers’ federation president says Australia ‘can’t even keep [illicit] cigarettes out of the country … let alone some of these difficult...
australia.content:
Years-old recommendations by Australia’s biosecurity watchdog have been ignored or not acted on by successive federal governments, increasing the risk of an invasive pest outbreak such as the fire ants discovered in Sydney this week, according to experts.

Environmentalists and biosecurity experts warn the large colony of red imported fire ants are a warning sign that the country’s quarantine system is too slow-moving, underfunded and overly concerned with agriculture.

The nest was found in Auburn and is the second outbreak of the invasive species in Sydney this year after they were discovered at the Enfield intermodal logistics centre on 23 September.

Both sites are industrial areas dealing with imported goods.

The NSW agriculture minister, Tara Moriarty, said on Wednesday that the Auburn outbreak was “different to what has occurred in the past and is seemingly the result of infested imported goods”.

“Our government is boosting our on-ground resources and establishing a taskforce to focus on tracing the supply chains that have led to this occurring,” she said.

But experts say there have been years of warnings about Australia’s biosecurity, often not acted on by the federal government, that might have made a difference in halting the ants’ spread.

The policy director of the Invasive Species Council, Carol Booth, pointed to a 2021 review by the inspector general of biosecurity of the controls for the Khapra beetle, which made recommendations to improve the entire quarantine system.

The South Asian beetle is the second-highest identified national priority plant pest, due to its risks to the grain industry.

At the time, the inspector general made 13 recommendations, including that the department “improve its level of regulatory agility”, “with an expectation of response time frames of days or weeks, not months or years” due to the rapidly-evolving risk of outbreak.

It also criticised the federal government for not acting when the risk of the beetle arriving was first identified in July 2020.

“This delay is an illustration of the department’s continuing regulatory immaturity,” the inspector general found, suggesting either a poorly defined risk assessment process or an overly cavalier attitude to risk.

Four years later, nothing had been done about the recommendation to improve response times. An October 2025 review of the report by the inspector general found that all but one of the recommendations were still open.

Booth said the recommendation was particularly significant because biosecurity risks to Australia were endlessly evolving and increasing, partly due to climate change.

“There are just so many things they should be doing that they’re not, or they weren’t doing well, or they weren’t auditing to ensure that their measures were being actually implemented,” Booth said.

“There’s definitely some things they do well, but others, they just don’t have the resources.”

The Guardian understands the recommendation has since been implemented.

Hamish McIntyre, the president of the National Farmers’ Federation, said farmers “believe we are watching a national biosecurity and human health disaster unfold in front of our eyes around fire ants” due to a failure of the quarantine system.

“We can’t even keep [illicit] cigarettes out of the country through our borders, let alone some of these difficult-to-detect pests.”

He said being an island nation was Australia’s greatest biosecurity advantage.

The federal minister for agriculture, Julie Collins, said the government had delivered over $2bn in additional biosecurity resourcing since 2022.

“This includes more than $296m in the current red imported fire ant eradication program,” she said.

“In the last financial year alone, federal biosecurity officers inspected almost 350,000 commercial sea and air cargoes, preventing tens of thousands of harmful pests, diseases and weeds from entering Australia.”

Tom Kompas, a professor of environmental economics and biosecurity at the University of Melbourne, said it was likely that Sydney’s infestation was broader than currently thought.

“If it does get into metro Sydney, it would be a disaster. It would be an absolute disaster,” he said.

Tax the importer

Australia has a reputation for extraordinarily tough and strict biosecurity controls, but no system can block, inspect or decontaminate every container of every pest.

“We’re going to have incursions of fire ants, among other things,” the Invasive Species Council CEO, Jack Gough, said.

“The key is basically how early in the biosecurity system we’re catching these things, such that then it’s a lot easier to deal with.”

While the Enfield site had been subject to pest inspections, Gough said there had been “clear failings” because its fire ant mitigation process did not match the ant’s biology.

Lures were only placed in some businesses once a year, but ants can move after six months, he said. They were also placed too far apart, further than the 40 or so metres the ants will roam.

He said this was partly due to underfunding and an overreliance on mitigation in the private sector.

Kompas said the biosecurity system was hampered by its approach to risk, with funding against an individual pest allocated according to concern levels. According to him, a better approach would be to allocate funding based on an assessment of cost effectiveness and suggested testing Australian cows for foot-and-mouth disease is probably overfunded.

He said the system placed an overemphasis on mitigating risks to agriculture rather than the environment.

Ultimately, it falls to the taxpayer to pay for eradication, Gough said. Queensland’s fire ant eradication program costs more than $100m a year.

The Invasive Species Council has long called for a new tax on importers to fund the country’s biosecurity system, but Gough said Australia’s obligations under World Trade Organization agreements had prevented its implementation as a flat fee.

australia.title: Barrie and Tony's final Victorian election predictions – Back to Back Barries live
australia.snippet: In this sold-out live show from the Capitol Theatre in Melbourne, Barrie Cassidy and Tony Barry give their final predictions for what is ...
australia.content: In this sold-out live show from the Capitol Theatre in Melbourne, Barrie Cassidy and Tony Barry give their final predictions for what is being called the most consequential state election in a generation. The Barries examine the latest polls and seats to watch, and give their take on how Victoria could change on Saturday night. They also discuss public frustration at Labor for the cost-of-living crisis and whether Chris Bowen should be blamed for Cop31's fossil fuel failure. This event was hosted by the Wheeler Centre and RMIT

australia.title: How now big cows: meet Frank and Tiny Tim, perhaps the largest cattle in Australia
australia.snippet: Saved from the slaughterhouse, the two behemoths are turning heads on opposite sides of the country, having grown to 192cm They’re taller...
australia.content:
They’re taller than Chris Hemsworth. They each weigh as much as a small car. And they are some of the biggest cattle Australia has ever seen.

Two massive steers, named Frank and Tiny Tim, have sparked headlines in recent days for being, well, big boys.

Krystal Camilleri, the co-founder of the bovine adoption agency Companion Cows, has cared for Frank, a Holstein Friesian steer, for six years after rescuing the animal from a dairy farm in the north of Tasmania. Like many male dairy calves, he was set to be slaughtered young.

Instead, Frank has grown into a behemoth in Camilleri’s paddock in southern Tasmania and recently prompted her veterinarian to declare him the biggest animal she had ever seen.

“He loves cuddles, he falls asleep on my lap and snores like a dog,” Camilleri told Guardian Australia.

Recent measurements – using a horse measuring stick – put Frank at 192cm at the shoulder, making him one of the tallest steers in the country. Camilleri says he’s a gentle giant and “just a big teddy bear”.

But Frank is not alone in his hugeness.

About 2,900km away, another large cow has been spotted. Eric Walmsley, a cattle farmer in Waroona, a small farming community about an hour south of Perth, has also had his own Friesian steer measured and weighed in recent days.

The animal, dubbed Tiny Tim, was too big for the abattoir and Walmsley decided to keep him as a pet on his farm. He’s now eight years old.

“We’ve had him since he was a day old,” Walmsley said. “He went in the paddock and over the years he got bigger and bigger, and all of a sudden I thought, jeez. It was really the last couple of years he’s shot up in height. He’s bloody big now.”

Tiny Tim also stands at 192cm at the shoulder. He was taken over the weigh bridge in a horse float and came in at about 1,400kg.

Walmsley said Tiny Tim was about double the size of the other Friesians in his herd and had a gentle nature. He was often kept in the front paddock near the road with his friend, a longhorn steer.

“It’s amazing the amount of people that pull up,” Walmsley said. “These blokes are very quiet, but they’re inquisitive, they’ll eat out of your hand.”

Walmsley said Tiny Tim was unique as many steers don’t get the chance to grow to full size because they’re headed for the abattoir.

Tiny Tim and Frank may be tied for the place of Australia’s biggest bovine after the death of Knickers, a very large Holstein Friesian. Knickers and owner Geoff Pearson found themselves the focus of the global media after a photo of Knickers standing in a paddock of much smaller cows went viral.

Knickers clocked in at 194cm, slightly taller than Frank and Tiny Tim. He died at a farm in Western Australia a few years ago.

The current tallest living steer, a Canadian Holstein Friesian named Beef, measures in at just under 196cm.

Camilleri said the two Australian steers are genetic anomalies that probably shouldn’t be as big as they are. She added that Frank will probably only live until about 10 as his massive bulk strains his joints and body. Cattle can live to be as old as 20.

Holstein Friesians have been selectively bred to produce huge quantities of milk and be large in size, but usually cap out at about 165cm.

“Frank’s size does shock a lot of people, but I didn’t do anything special to get him to this size,” Camilleri said.

“There’s actually nothing unique about these big cows, they’ve just been left to grow to their full potential.”

She said she hoped Frank’s story would help shed light on issues in the dairy industry when it comes to male calves.

“I just loved him and respected him.”

world.title: ‘I’m no longer a UAE official’: UN hopeful Lana Nusseibeh tries to shake off Sudan record
world.snippet: The US and Russia’s candidate for secretary general is on a charm offensive. Can she overcome London’s resistance to her bid? Lana Nussei...
world.content:
Lana Nusseibeh is in Britain this week, attempting to present herself as a potential future UN secretary general, and shift the focus from her past as a United Arab Emirates diplomat who denied the country’s role in arming a militia accused of war crimes and genocide in Sudan’s four-year civil war.

It is a high-risk strategy that involves meeting ministers, MPs, academics and holding a public event with the UN Association.

Labelled by many British NGOs and others as an apologist for war crimes, Nusseibeh is presenting herself as a skilled diplomat with the network to put the UN back at the centre of mediation, development and human rights.

“These are very geopolitical times,” she said in an interview. “You need a geopolitical secretary general, because the fact is these geopolitical ruptures are not going away. These fissures in the international system are not going to dissolve any time soon.”

Nusseibeh had a setback last Friday, when three permanent members of the UN security council, China, France and the UK, all voted to “discourage” her candidature. The UN’s electoral system requires that she secure nine positive votes from the 15-strong security council, and no discouragement from the permanent five (P5) before being recommended to the UN general assembly.

She has the backing of the US and Russia, and thinks her cause is not lost. “Sometimes, the use of the veto is tactical. Sometimes, it’s a holding position, sometimes it’s a leveraging position. There are a number of different theories”.

The centre of the resistance to Nusseibeh’s candidacy is probably London, and specifically the Foreign Office, the penholder on Sudan at the UN, and this may explain the UK political blitz.

When questioned about her role in Sudan, she asked that her candidacy be seen in the round, highlighting her role in forcing humanitarian aid into Gaza, her support for Afghan women and promoting interfaith tolerance.

“Like every candidate, I come from somewhere, but the independence of the incoming secretary general is the key to their credibility.

“I’ve taken a leave of absence from my role in [the] UAE government in order to independently campaign for this role. But I think that if I was secretary general, Sudan would be the litmus test of success for any incoming secretary because it’s such a horrific humanitarian crisis.”

The war in Sudan, which erupted in April 2023 after a power struggle between the ​military and the Rapid Support Forces, has displaced more than 14 million people and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. Multiple regional powers, including the UAE, have backed different local proxies since the beginning of the conflict in an attempt to win influence and strategic resources.

The UAE has long been accused of supporting the RSF in Sudan, a charge repeatedly denied by Nusseibeh, who has publicly disputed the findings of UN investigators.

A UN panel of experts suggested last month that the UAE had supplied crucial support to the RSF.

Asked if she regretted dissembling during her time as a diplomat, by denying the UAE had armed the RSF, or her personal role in challenging the UN reports critical of the UAE, Nusseibeh said she regretted that “the Sudanese civil war had continued for so long”.

Nusseibeh added: “But I don’t think saying that is enough for the Sudanese people and the people in the surrounding countries where they’ve also felt the impact of this war, or for the victims of sexual violence and in this conflict, the atrocities committed in El Fasher without accountability, and the use of chemical weapons against the civilian population; all of these are a litany of suffering that has been inflicted on the Sudanese people.”

Asked if the UAE had been supplying weapons to the RSF in a breach of a UN embargo, she replied: “I’m aware of the allegations. I haven’t read the last UN panel of experts report, but I’m not going to comment as I’m no longer a UAE official. In this campaign, I am a secretary general candidate.

“As secretary general, I would fully back the findings of all UN panel of experts reports and I’m aware that I think several countries have been mentioned in various reports.”She later added: “I would call out countries that are supplying arms to any of the parties, including those in the RSF … this needs a process that requires accountability for atrocities that have been committed. That it needs to be a process primarily led by the Sudanese people.”

Nusseibeh said she was willing to take risks to mediate and to put UN values, expertise and its development toolkit at the centre of disputes. Her analysis of contemporary diplomacy was that the world had descended into a default setting of non-cooperation, and the UN needed to restate the case for collaboration between nations as being in the self-interest of everyone.

The UN had been missing from too many conflicts, she argued, and she would set up a mediation board to try to use the full UN toolkit, ranging from confidence-building measures to development to secure peace. “What’s missing is this idea of a secretary general that is a strategist and a mediator-in-chief that is looking at the sort of the blips on the dashboard of conflict and saying, ‘How do we deploy to have maximum impact for most effective use of resource and cost?’ Because resources are not going up, they’re going down. I mean, we’re looking at, since 2010, 40% increase in military spending. So we’re using a lot of hard power as countries and systems to deter, but it’s not actually working.”

That would require some prioritisation at the UN – it has 4,000 different open mandates.

Her intelligence and skills as a diplomat are not in question. However, her track record over Sudan is.

One critic said: “It is a very smart strategic play by the UAE that seeks autocratic capture, and then the asset-stripping of the UN and its standards. The UAE would end the UN’s role on climate. It would be a catastrophe.”

The next security council vote is on Monday. By then some of the backmarkers may have dropped out of the race. The diplomats of the P5 may also be clearer on the flexibility of their mandates, in which case the papal conclave may finally produce white smoke.

world.title: At least 31 killed as fuel tanker crash ignites large fire on Cairo highway
world.snippet: Blaze on ring road surrounding Egyptian capital injures at least 21 people and leaves cars and motorcycles charred A crash involving a fu...
world.content:
A crash involving a fuel tanker ignited a huge fire on a highway surrounding Cairo on Wednesday, killing at least 31 people, Egyptian authorities said.

The blaze on the ring road, a key artery that encircles the Egyptian capital, also injured at least 21 people and left more than two dozen cars and motorcycles charred, according to the latest figures released by the health ministry.

State media reported that the fire broke out when the fuel truck overturned. The stretch of the highway where it occurred was in Waraq, a densely populated neighbourhood in Giza, part of the Greater Cairo area, the health ministry said.

At the scene, rescue workers were pulling people out of burning cars. An Associated Press video showed firefighters working to put out the fire spreading among the cars. Hundreds of people gathered near the scene.

Ahmed Sameer, who was stuck in traffic as the road was blocked after the accident, saw the fuel truck and many cars on fire. He said he saw at least eight bodies being removed from burned cars.

“It was a huge fire, the cars got stuck together because of the fire,” he said, describing the fear and panic that followed. “It was a shocking scene.”

The Egyptian president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, expressed his condolences to the victims in a statement. The public prosecutor’s office said DNA investigations were under way to identify the victims.

The health minister, Khaled Abdel Ghaffar, said the injured were taken to nearby hospitals and that the death toll was preliminary, raising concerns it could rise further. He later travelled to the scene and to the hospitals, the health ministry said.

The minister’s spokesperson told the state-linked Al-Qahera News that the ring road had been reopened and the remnants of the accident cleared.

Deadly traffic incidents claim thousands of lives every year in Egypt, which has a poor transportation safety record. Speeding, bad roads and poor enforcement of traffic laws are the main reasons behind most of the crashes.

In January 2016, 21 people were killed and 16 were injured in a multicar pileup on a road near the southern province of Beni Suef.

world.title: Swiss tourist killed and British and Americans injured by elephants in Cameroon
world.snippet: Alain Throo, insurance executive based in London, reportedly gored and later died on hike near Mount Cameroon national park A Swiss touri...
world.content:
A Swiss tourist has been killed and British and American tourists have been injured when a group of hikers encountered a herd of elephants in Cameroon.

The group of six tourists, four British, one Swiss and one American, accompanied by local guides, were hiking near the village of Bakingili in the south of the Mount Cameroon national park on 19 November, on a path used by elephants to access a nearby lake, when they encountered the herd of about 15 animals, according to media reports.

The elephants attacked the group and Alain Throo, a Swiss insurance executive based in London, was reportedly gored and one of the guides tossed into a ditch on top of Throo, while the others hid in trees.

Throo had a black eye and was initially responsive and complaining about an injury to his arm, one of the British female hikers told Cameroonian media, which said they had feared he was bleeding internally.

“He said that the elephant attacked him,” an unidentified Cameroonian man added, according to a video posted by CBS Radio Buea FM. “It smashed him.”

Throo later died of his injuries and his body was carried out of the park by a combined team of park staff and the military to a mortuary in the town of Limbeon 21 November. The American hiker was treated at the same hospital and later discharged, according to local media.

One of the British tourists, who said he had hid in a tree stump for two hours, recalled the moment the elephants attacked their group. “I saw these elephants almost next to me. And I thought, if I go down this path as well, I’m going to get hit. So I just moved to the opposite direction. They ran down the path, I ran and hid in a bush. And I heard some screaming.”

Sean McGovern, the UK chief executive of the insurer Axa XL, where Throo had worked for 13 years, confirmed the death, saying Throo was a “valued member of our team, respected colleague and friend whose contribution, professionalism and warmth touched many people”.

Cameroonian media reported that clashes between elephants and local people had been happening for the past 10 years.

Mount Cameroon is the highest mountain in west and central Africa, at more than 4,000 metres. The African forest elephant was declared critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature in 2021. There are about 195,000 left in the wild, less than 15% of its population 50 years ago, according to the World Wildlife Fund.

Just 5% of forest elephants, which are smaller than their savannah-based counterparts, are found outside central Africa. In Cameroon, there are about 6,000 forest elephants, according to the NGO Global Conservation, which said the species was at risk from poaching syndicates.

A spokesperson for Britain’s Foreign Office said: “We offered assistance after a number of British nationals were injured in Cameroon.”

world.title: Sri Lankan asylum seeker killed himself after being sent by UK to Eswatini
world.snippet: Kishanth Peramalya was denied entry due to sexual assault convictions and sent to Africa where he had no connections The UK sent a Sri La...
world.content:
The UK sent a Sri Lankan asylum seeker who had been convicted of sexual assault to Eswatini, a southern African country to which he had no connection and where he killed himself.

Kishanth Peramalya was part of a group that set sail from India hoping to reach Canada and claim asylum there. The boat was rescued by the Royal Navy in October 2021 when it got into difficulty and brought to Diego Garcia in the remote British Indian Ocean Territory, which hosts a US-UK military base.

In November 2024, the UK allowed 61 migrants to enter from Diego Garcia after a damning UN report about conditions in the camp. However, the then home secretary, Yvette Cooper, denied Peramalya entry to the UK due to his criminal convictions while he was on Diego Garcia for four counts of sexual assault, one count of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and one count of arson. Cooper’s decision was upheld by UK courts.

Peramalya had been granted protection from being returned to Sri Lanka, having been tortured and sexually abused by Sri Lankan military personnel as a teenager. In late March, the Maldives said it would take him for 30 days, according to the BBC. He was then transferred to Eswatini, a country landlocked by South Africa and Mozambique and formerly known as Swaziland, where he killed himself on 13 September.

A draft deal between the UK and Eswatini governments would have committed Downing Street to cover the costs of Peramalya’s resettlement there for three years, according to the BBC, which said the UK was also finalising arrangements for Peramalya to live in Eswatini permanently.

The Guardian has not seen the draft deal. Thabile Mdluli, a spokesperson for Eswatini’s government, said: “The initial arrangement was temporary in nature and intended to safeguard Mr Peramalya’s safety while the government of the United Kingdom worked towards a long-term solution regarding his circumstances.”

She said that no formal agreement was ever reached over Peramalya’s long-term residency status with the UK and declined to comment further on the specific arrangements of his stay in Eswatini or the circumstances around his death.

Mdluli said: “Eswatini has not received any other similar request from the government of the United Kingdom. The government of the Kingdom of Eswatini remains committed to ensuring that any agreements entered into with external partners safeguard national interest as well as the safety and security of Emaswati [Swazi people].”

A UK government spokesperson said: “Keeping the British public safe will always be our first priority, and we will continue to take the decisions necessary to protect the British people. That includes taking steps to ensure high harm foreign criminals cannot enter the UK. We continue to work with the Eswatini authorities in relation to this case.”

Peramalya had post-traumatic stress disorder and attempted suicide multiple times on Diego Garcia, according to a UK high court judgment in February 2025.

Peramalya’s family told the BBC he was initially housed alone in an isolated guesthouse in Eswatini. “My brother did not want to go there at all,” said his sister, speaking from India. “He couldn’t manage being there alone, he was very lonely.”

She said he had called her four times a day and was initially having weekly psychiatric appointments, which were made daily when his mental health deteriorated, as well as having someone brought in to prepare his food.

Peramalya’s relatives said they were not aware of his convictions for sexual offences or any plan to make his transfer to Eswatini permanent.

Eswatini has accepted dozens of third-country deportees from the US since July 2025. In November 2025, its government confirmed it had received $5.1m in exchange for taking up to 160 migrants from the US.

world.title: More than 300 Russians killed as Moscow props up Mali’s junta, leaked data reveals
world.snippet: Exclusive: Records list 349 deaths in three years in Mali and also shed light on Russia’s military activity elsewhere in Africa When the ...
world.content:
When the attack on Kidal began before dawn on 25 April this year, the Russian fighters were caught off guard. Within the first hour, checkpoints on the outskirts of the remote desert city nestled among the rocky hills of northern Mali had fallen to the insurgents, who pushed towards the police station where fierce fighting erupted.

“Everything was happening at once. Explosions were going off all around us, people were shouting,” recalled a former member of Russia’s Africa Corps who was stationed in Mali at the time and spoke on condition of anonymity. “Nobody knew where the enemy was coming from.”

The Kremlin-controlled forces and their Malian allies were facing a coordinated surprise assault by the al-Qaida-linked JNIM and the Tuareg-led Azawad Liberation Front (FLA), whose fighters used suicide car bombs and drones to break through the city’s defences.

Leaked Russian state records suggest the losses were heavy that day. Death certificates of Russian fighters killed in Mali, held by Rosstat, Russia’s state statistics agency, were obtained by the hacker groups Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow and analysed by the Guardian.

The records show that 43 Russians died in Mali on 25 April, including six in Kidal and one in nearby Aguelhok. Others were recorded as dying in the capital, Bamako, and in Gao, where rebels shot down a Russian military helicopter that day.

By the following morning, the Russians had abandoned Kidal, which Russian mercenaries had helped capture in November 2023 and which Moscow had since held up as a showcase of its growing influence in Africa.

In all, the records list 349 Russian deaths in Mali between September 2023 and September 2026, most of which the Guardian was able to link to known battles with rebel groups.

The figures offer a previously unseen glimpse into the human cost of Moscow’s efforts to prop up Mali’s military junta, in what has become Russia’s largest military deployment in Africa.

Two western officials who have travelled to Mali and were shown the data said the death toll was higher than previously estimated.

“That’s over 10% of Russia’s forces killed in action,” said one of the officials, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to comment publicly.

Moscow does not publish its losses in Africa, and its foreign ministry did not respond to a request for comment.

The Wagner private military group, led by the warlord Yevgeny Prigozhin, first arrived in Mali in late 2021, a year after a military coup had toppled President Ibrahim Boubacar Keïta. French forces were ordered to leave the country as relations with the junta deteriorated, bringing an end to France’s decade-long counter-terrorism operation and leaving Russia as the regime’s main foreign protector.

Wagner handed over its operations in Mali to the Africa Corps in June 2025, two years after Prigozhin led a failed mutiny on Moscow that discredited the group in the eyes of the Kremlin. By that summer, British intelligence estimated that about 2,000 Africa Corps personnel were deployed in the country.

The Africa Corps, closely overseen by Russian military intelligence, currently provides backing to several African governments in return for payment or lucrative contracts granting access to natural resources.

Despite the Russian presence, Mali’s security situation has continued to deteriorate. In late July 2024, Russian and Malian forces fought Tuareg separatists for several days near Tinzaouaten, on the Algerian border.

Wagner at the time issued a rare statement admitting losses, including the death of a commander, but gave no figure. Estimates from Russian sources ranged from about 20 to more than 80 dead.

The Rosstat records list 70 Russians who died on 27 July 2024, all but one of them in the Kidal region. The figures make the battle of Tinzaouaten the deadliest single day for Russian forces in Africa since Wagner mercenaries first deployed to the continent in 2017.

The toll in Mali may have been driven up by Ukraine, which has extended its war against Russia to the Sahel. Kyiv has been assisting Tuareg rebels there, according to two people with knowledge of the operations. CNN has reported that about 15 Ukrainian specialists were deployed to Mali to help local rebel forces fighting Russian troops.

The records are probably an undercount. Registration often lags, and no Russian deaths in Mali are recorded for March 2026 although at least three Africa Corps fighters were reported killed in an ambush near Nampala that month.

The leaked data also sheds light on Russia’s military activity elsewhere in Africa. Central African Republic, where Wagner fighters guard the president, Faustin-Archange Touadéra, accounts for 30 deaths. While not all could be linked to known incidents, three men died on the night drones struck Wagner camps in Kaga-Bandoro in December 2023.

In Libya, where Russian forces back the eastern commander Khalifa Haftar and use his airbases as a supply route to their deployments in the Sahel, some of the recorded deaths were probably linked to a helicopter crash at the Maaten al-Sarra base in February 2026. On Sunday, Ukrainian drones sunk a Russian warship off the coast of Libya; it is unclear whether there were any casualties.

In Niger, where Russia’s Africa Corps moved in after the military junta expelled French and US troops, a Russian fighter died two days after Islamic State militants attacked Niamey airport in January, a previously unreported casualty.

Moscow has in recent months stepped up its effort to show it is back in control in Mali. On 6 October, Malian troops and the Africa Corps recaptured Kidal after what the army called an air and ground campaign.

A report this month by the US-based Conflict Insights Group (CIG) found that the Africa Corps had sharply increased its use of drones in Mali, including Lancet suicide drones, amid an intensifying air campaign.

The group wrote that the drone campaign had also targeted civilians, boostering support for the rebels. “Civilian deaths in the intensified air campaign, which the Africa Corps leads, are likely to aid insurgent recruitment,” it said.


A western diplomat who works in the region said the attacks in late April had punctured the image of Russian military invincibility that Moscow and the junta had cultivated among Malians.

“Russia still wields considerable influence in Mali, but patience with its military performance is wearing thin.”
